title: Aaron Driver's 'more powerful' bomb never exploded, RCMP says, revealing new details of tense confrontation
subtitle: Only Driver's detonators exploded, RCMP said. The ISIL supporter said Allahu Akbar before police shot him, thinking he was trying to detonate the more powerful bombs
article: TORONTO-The bomb that ISIL supporter Aaron Driver tried to trigger inside his taxi when he was confronted by police on Aug. 10 never fully detonated, RCMP Deputy Commissioner Mike Cabana said in an interview Saturday.

Police now believe the blast in the cab was caused by the detonators and that the more powerful explosives never actually ignited, he said, although Cabana added the forensic investigation of the homemade bomb was still underway.

"Primary indications are the only thing that exploded were the homemade detonators," Cabana, the deputy commissioner for federal policing, told the National Post. "The forensics are going to confirm that but that's what it looks like."

The explosive substance appears to be the same type that police found a formula for making on Driver's computer when they searched his home in Winnipeg on June 3, 2015. "I think so but I don't think the forensics are complete on that, but I think essentially he followed the same recipe."

The target of his alleged attack has still not been determined, he added. While Driver had told the taxi driver to take him to Citi Plaza in London, Ont., there is no indication that was the target and Cabana noted there was a train station near the mall.
"Was he going there to hop on the train? We don't know yet so we're doing the forensics on the computer, hoping that we're going to find something there but so far we have nothing," he said.

Ten days after Driver was killed by police in Strathroy, Ont., as he was allegedly about to conduct a bombing, the deputy commissioner provided a detailed update on what investigators now believe happened and what they have learned so far.

Cabana said the initial tip that came from the FBI only indicated that the U.S. had "come in possession" of a video that appeared to link directly to Canada. "Probably primarily because the first few words were O Canada," he said.

The FBI passed on about a half-dozen "indicators" of the masked man's identity, such as that he was in his early 20s and spoke English. The RCMP went through a list of "individuals of interest" and came up with 11 suspects. Upon receiving a still image taken from the video, the list was narrowed to five.

But one of the analysts was certain he recognized the balaclava in the video. After comparing it to news photos of Driver leaving court in Winnipeg, and analyzing his eyes and the balaclava, they were fairly sure it was him.

"The moment that they narrowed down that they believed it could be Driver" surveillance teams were sent to his residence and workplace, Cabana said. While they still didn't have confirmation, "we didn't want to take any chances."

Meanwhile, the RCMP obtained the actual video at 11 to 11:30 a.m., he said. The audio portion was sent to investigators in Manitoba who had spoken to Driver and they thought it was him. An Emergency Response Team was dispatched. "There was a significant number of resources that were on their way to Strathroy."

The surveillance team was still trying to determine if Driver was at home when a taxi pulled into the driveway at 4:18 p.m., he said. Also at 4:18, Driver came out carrying a backpack and got into the cab and it began to reverse towards the street.
"He didn't get to move very far," Cabana said.

Driver tried to detonate his explosives and there was a blast, he said. Photos released by the RCMP show little damage to the interior of the cab. The cabbie sitting behind the wheel suffered minor injuries and Driver himself survived.

"Subsequent to that he came out of the cab and was standing up and was not following the direction that was provided and was playing - and again all of that's going to be confirmed, this is all based on preliminary information - but he was playing with his backpack and his chest, touching his chest in the front."

Cabana said Driver said Allahu Akbar, "God is great." Apparently concerned he was still trying to detonate the explosives, police shot him. "The members didn't take any chances." He was hit by two bullets, according to his father.

The apparent close-call has led to debate about terrorism peace bonds, which police have been using to restrict suspected extremists. A judge had approved a peace bond against Driver but he was not under surveillance.

"The peace bonds, I think they're good," Cabana said. "I think they help but I think there are things missing in terms of authorities associated with the peace bond that would be helpful. Actually without it, it really diminishes the capacity of the peace bond.

"If he was communicating with people and we didn't have the authority to monitor his communication, which was the case here, well then you can put any restriction. If nobody's keeping an eye or checking that does very little."

He said peace bonds might also include a verification aspect, giving police and security agencies the power to monitor electronic transmissions from the suspect to make sure he is complying with the terms imposed by the court.

The taxi driver, Terry Duffield, said in interviews this week he had no idea a police operation was underway until the tactical team confronted Driver. He said he should have been stopped before reaching Driver's house.

"In the initial hours of this thing we didn't know if he (Driver) was home," Cabana responded. "We didn't know who else was there. It might have been somebody else in the residence. So our position at that point in time was very much to put surveillance on the place to make sure we could keep on eye on who was coming and going.

"And if we saw him the order had been passed if you see him arrest him. But for all we knew he might have been away from the residence coming back. So it was important for us to be as inconspicuous as possible. When the taxi showed up, the taxi showed up."

He said it was "very unfortunate that he was put in that position and if we could have prevented it we would have prevented it." But he said an Ontario Provincial Police investigation would reconstruct exactly what happened.

"Like everything like this there's always lessons learned, so we're going to go through this, we're going to have a look at the OPP report and see if there's anything that could or should have been done differently. We're going to own up to this if we did something wrong. But right now preliminary indications seems to be that everything was done by the book."
